levels.title: Dock Numbers
levels.story: The parcel has crossed the ranch. Now Kit stands in the Harbour of Ports, where ships arrive by the hundred and the harbourmaster sorts them by dock number.

everyday.scene: A large office building has one street address. Inside, each company has its own suite number, and the front desk sends every visitor to the right suite.
everyday.question: The street address got you to the building. What gets you to the right company?
everyday.answer: The suite number. A computer is the same: the IP address finds the machine, and a port number finds the program inside it that should receive the data.

lessons.title: The address and the suite
text: The network layer delivers packets from one machine to another. The transport layer goes one step further: from one program to another. A port is a 16-bit number that names a program on a machine, like a suite number inside a building.

A connection is identified by four values: source IP, source port, destination IP and destination port. Many conversations can share one machine, because the four values differ. Some ports are well known: 22 is SSH, 25 is mail, 53 is name lookups, 80 is the web and 443 is the secure web.

terms.meaning: A 16-bit number that names a program on a machine.
Many conversations sharing one machine and one network address.
A running program.

predict.prompt: Two browser tabs on the same laptop open the same website. Which of the four connection values differ?
predict.answer: The source port. The laptop uses a different one for each connection.

deeper.title: Who picks the client's port?
text: A server listens on a well-known port so clients can find it. A client does not need a fixed port, so its operating system picks an unused high-numbered one for each connection.

references.title: Peterson & Davie, Computer Networks: A Systems Approach, End-to-End Protocols
Wikipedia: List of TCP and UDP port numbers

lessons.title: Two ways to ship
text: UDP just sends. It has no set-up, no resends and no ordering, and its header is only 8 bytes: source port, destination port, length and checksum. It is quick and simple.
TCP first sets up a connection, then delivers a reliable, in-order stream of bytes, resending anything that goes missing. That costs set-up time and extra work.
Choose UDP when speed matters more than perfection, such as live calls and games. Choose TCP when every byte must arrive.

terms.meaning: Connectionless and unreliable, but fast and simple.
Connection-based, reliable and in order.

predict.prompt: A UDP packet carries a 120-byte message. What goes in its length field?
predict.answer: 128. The length counts the 8-byte header as well as the data.

references.title: Peterson & Davie, Computer Networks: A Systems Approach, Simple Demultiplexer (UDP)

lessons.title: Opening a dock
text: Programs talk to the transport layer through sockets. A server prepares in four steps: socket creates the socket, bind claims a port number, listen starts waiting for visitors, and accept takes the next arriving connection.
A client has it easier. It calls socket, then connect, naming the server's address and port. After that both sides can send and receive, and finally close.

terms.meaning: A door a program uses to send and receive over the network.
Wait for incoming connections on a port.

predict.prompt: Which call does a server make that a client does not?
predict.answer: bind, listen and accept. A client only calls socket and connect.

references.title: Peterson & Davie, Computer Networks: A Systems Approach, End-to-End Protocols

fieldNotes.title: Where the client's port comes from
fieldNotes.text: When your laptop opens a connection, its operating system picks an unused high-numbered port as the source port. The exact range depends on the operating system, so a server never knows in advance what a client's port will be.

source.title: RFC 6335: IANA Procedures for Port Numbers

fieldNotes.verifyNote: Check the claim that the range depends on the OS (IANA suggests 49152-65535; some systems use other ranges).

summary: You learned that ports turn machine-to-machine delivery into program-to-program delivery, compared UDP with TCP, and put a server's socket calls in order.
The harbourmaster stamps the manifest. "Dock sorted," she says. "But your parcel needs a proper introduction before it is handed over."

mistake.title: Thinking an IP address is enough
mistake.text: An IP address gets data to the machine. Without a port, the machine would not know which of its programs should receive the data.

levels.title: The Handshake
levels.story: Before any parcel is handed over, the harbourmaster wants a proper introduction. Kit learns why ships must greet each other first, and what to do when a ghost ship drifts in.

everyday.scene: Before you give a stranger a phone number to call you back on, you say "Hello, it is Kit." They say "Hello, Kit, it is Sam." You say "Hi, Sam." Now both of you know the other is real and listening.
everyday.question: Why bother with three steps, not one?
everyday.answer: One hello proves nothing about who is listening. Three steps let each side check that the other heard it, and both can prove the conversation is new, not an echo of an old one.

lessons.title: Why not just start?
text: Old packets can wander the network and turn up late. If a server accepted every connection request it saw, a stale one from an old conversation could open a ghost connection, with nobody there to use it.

So each side picks its own starting sequence number, a number that labels the bytes it sends. Each side then confirms the other's number. A stale packet carries the wrong numbers, and its reply fails to match anything the sender remembers.

terms.meaning: A number that labels the bytes a side is sending.
An old copy of a packet that arrives long after it was sent.

predict.prompt: Why would a server be fooled by a delayed duplicate of an old connection request?
predict.answer: It cannot tell the old request from a new one unless something checks that the sender still wants it.

references.title: Peterson & Davie, Computer Networks: A Systems Approach, Transmission Control Protocol

lessons.title: The three steps
text: TCP's three-way handshake is SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. The client sends SYN with a starting number x. The server replies SYN-ACK with its own number y, and an acknowledgement of x + 1, meaning "the next number I expect from you". The client finishes with ACK of y + 1.

Example: x = 4000 and y = 9000. SYN has seq 4000. SYN-ACK has seq 9000 and ack 4001. The final ACK has seq 4001 and ack 9001. Once data flows, the numbers count bytes: 100 bytes from seq 4001 means the next byte is 4101.

terms.meaning: A message that opens a connection and carries a starting number.
A confirmation that says which number comes next.

predict.prompt: The server's SYN-ACK says seq = 9000. What ack does the client's final message carry?
predict.answer: 9001. It names the next number the client expects from the server.

deeper.title: The ghost fails
text: A ghost SYN from an old conversation reaches the server, which replies with a SYN-ACK. The client checks the ack number against the SYN it actually sent. It does not match, so the client rejects the reply with a reset (RST), and the server drops the half-open connection.

references.title: Peterson & Davie, Computer Networks: A Systems Approach, Transmission Control Protocol

lessons.title: Saying goodbye, and the two armies
text: To close, each direction ends separately: one side sends FIN and the other answers ACK, then the same the other way round. Ending one direction first lets the last data finish.

There is a deeper puzzle. Two ferry captains must sail at dawn together, but messengers may be lost on the way. Captain A sends "sail at dawn". B replies. But B cannot know A got the reply. Every confirmation needs its own confirmation, so perfect certainty is impossible.
Real protocols settle for timers and a limited number of retries.

terms.meaning: A message that says "I have no more to send".
A decision to give up after waiting long enough.

predict.prompt: Captain B sends the last confirmation. Can B be sure that it arrived?
predict.answer: No. The last message might be lost, and adding another confirmation just moves the same problem.

references.title: Peterson & Davie, Computer Networks: A Systems Approach, Transmission Control Protocol

fieldNotes.title: Unpredictable starting numbers
fieldNotes.text: Starting sequence numbers are not simply 0 or 1. Modern systems choose them in a hard-to-guess way, partly so that a stranger who cannot see your traffic cannot easily forge packets into your connection.

source.title: RFC 6528: Defending against Sequence Number Attacks

fieldNotes.verifyNote: Check that this one-line summary of RFC 6528 is fair.

summary: You followed a three-way handshake with real numbers, caught a ghost ship by checking the ack, and met the two-army problem.
The harbourmaster nods. "A proper introduction," she says. "Now there is the question of how much cargo the harbour can take before it jams."

mistake.title: Thinking the ack repeats the sequence number
mistake.text: The ack names the next number expected, one more than what was received. A SYN with seq 4000 is acknowledged with 4001.

levels.title: Traffic Jam
levels.story: The harbour road is jammed. Every ship wants to go at once, and the more they push, the slower everyone moves. Kit has to learn how senders can ease off without a traffic controller.

everyday.scene: At a school gate, parents all arrive at once and the road blocks. Everyone toots, cars creep, and fewer children get home than if everyone had arrived calmly.
everyday.question: How could each driver help, with no police officer in charge?
everyday.answer: Each driver can notice the jam and ease off, then slowly speed up again. No one is in charge, but everyone adjusts. TCP senders do just that.

lessons.title: Two different worries
text: Flow control protects the receiver. The receiver says how much room its buffer has (its window), and the sender never sends more than that. Congestion control protects the network in the middle.
A TCP sender keeps a second limit, the congestion window or cwnd, which it guesses from how well delivery is going. It may have in flight only the smaller of the two numbers.
Without congestion control, a busy network can reach congestion collapse: so many packets and resends that the good traffic actually falls.

terms.meaning: Keeping the sender from overwhelming the receiver.
Keeping senders from overwhelming the network.
The congestion window: how much the sender may have in flight.

predict.prompt: The receiver's window is 30 segments and the congestion window is 24. How many may the sender have in flight?

references.title: Peterson & Davie, Computer Networks: A Systems Approach, Congestion Control

lessons.title: Start slow, then creep
text: A new connection does not know how much the network can carry, so it starts small: cwnd of 1 segment. In slow start, the window doubles every round trip, until it reaches the threshold.

Past the threshold, it grows by 1 segment per round trip. This is additive increase. When a loss shows the network is full, the sender cuts back sharply, which is multiplicative decrease. Climb slowly, fall fast. Together this is AIMD, and the graph looks like a sawtooth.

terms.meaning: Doubling the window every round trip, from a small start.
The point where doubling stops and gentle growth begins.
Additive increase, multiplicative decrease.

predict.prompt: Why is it called slow start when the window doubles every round?
predict.answer: It starts small, at 1 segment. Doubling is fast growth from a very low starting point.

deeper.title: Why the window cannot jump back to where it was
text: A loss is a clue that the old size was too much. Cutting the threshold to half is a way to say "last time I got in trouble at 20, so doubling past 10 is risky".

references.title: Peterson & Davie, Computer Networks: A Systems Approach, Congestion Control

lessons.title: Two ways to react to a loss
text: A loss shows up two ways. A timeout means nothing is getting through. Three duplicate ACKs mean the receiver keeps asking for the same missing segment, so later segments are still arriving.

TCP Tahoe treats both the same: threshold = cwnd ÷ 2, cwnd = 1, then slow start again. TCP Reno is gentler on duplicate ACKs. It resends the missing segment at once (fast retransmit), sets the threshold to cwnd ÷ 2, and sets cwnd to the threshold (fast recovery). A timeout still sends Reno back to 1.

terms.meaning: Repeated acknowledgements for the same number, hinting at one missing segment.
Resending the missing segment without waiting for a timeout.

predict.prompt: Both Tahoe and Reno see 3 duplicate ACKs at cwnd = 20. What is each one's new cwnd?

references.title: Peterson & Davie, Computer Networks: A Systems Approach, Congestion Control

Protects the network in the middle

hints: Ask: who is being protected, the receiver or the network?
The receiver tells the sender its window.
activities.explain: Flow control is about the receiver. Congestion control is about everything in between.

activities.prompt: Build the sawtooth round by round, and predict the window each time.

steps.say: A new connection starts with a congestion window (cwnd) of 1 segment. The threshold, shown in the top bar, is 16. Each bar below it is one round trip.
Slow start: the window doubles each round, so 2.
Doubles again: 4.
Doubles again: 8.
Doubles to 16, which is the threshold.

predict.prompt: The congestion window is 8, and the threshold is 16. Still slow start, so the window doubles each round. What is it next round?
hints: In slow start the window doubles each round trip.
8 times 2.

steps.say: Past the threshold. Growth is now additive: just 1 segment per round. 17.

predict.prompt: The window has reached the threshold, 16. From here it grows by 1 segment per round. What is it next?
hints: Above the threshold, growth is additive.
16 plus 1.

steps.say: 20. The network is nearly full.
A timeout. A segment vanished and no acknowledgement came back. The network is jammed. The window drops to 1, and the threshold becomes half of 20.

predict.prompt: A timeout hits when the window is 20. What are the new threshold and window?
hints: The threshold is halved.
After a timeout the sender starts again from 1 segment.

steps.say: Round 10: the window is back at 1. Slow start begins again, with a threshold of 10.
10. It stops doubling at the threshold, and growth turns additive. The sawtooth is complete: climb, drop, climb again.

activities.explain: Build the sawtooth round by round, and predict the window each time.

activities.prompt: The receiver advertises a window of 30 segments and the congestion window is 24. How many segments may be in flight?
hints: Both limits apply.
Take the smaller number.
activities.explain: The sender obeys both limits, so it uses the smaller: 24.

activities.prompt: A connection is in slow start with cwnd = 4 and a threshold of 32. After 3 more round trips with no loss, what is cwnd?
hints: It doubles each round while below the threshold.
activities.explain: 4 doubles to 8, 16 and then 32, which is the threshold.

activities.prompt: A timeout occurs when cwnd = 24. What is the new threshold?

activities.explain: The threshold is halved: 12. cwnd drops to 1.

activities.prompt: Reno gets 3 duplicate ACKs when cwnd = 20. What is its cwnd afterwards?
hints: Reno halves the window and keeps going from there.
It does not restart at 1 for duplicate ACKs.
activities.explain: Reno sets the threshold to 10 and cwnd to 10, then grows additively.

activities.prompt: Put one tooth of the sawtooth in order.
items: Slow start: the window doubles each round
Additive increase: grow by 1 per round
A loss shows the network is full

hints: Doubling comes before gentle growth.
The cut comes after the loss.
activities.explain: Double, reach the threshold, creep, notice loss, cut back.

feed.explain: The receiver's window limits the sender. Congestion control protects the network.

feed.prompt: What does the window do in slow start?
feed.explain: It starts small, then grows quickly until the threshold.

fieldNotes.title: The sawtooth in real life
fieldNotes.text: Real TCP does not behave exactly like Tahoe or Reno. Many modern systems use other algorithms, and CUBIC is a common default on Linux. They all keep the same idea: probe for room, and back off when the network pushes back.
fieldNotes.verifyNote: Check that CUBIC is the Linux default and that the one-line summary is fair.

summary: You separated flow control from congestion control, built a sawtooth round by round, and compared how Tahoe and Reno react to loss.

The harbour road clears. The parcel arrives whole at the far dock, and Farmer Juno's door is in sight. But when Kit looks at the door, there is no name on it, only a number. "Where do I take this?" Kit wonders.

mistake.title: Mixing up the two windows
mistake.text: The receiver's window and the congestion window are different limits, set by different things. The sender obeys whichever is smaller.
